items.q: A pharmaceutical researcher tests a newly discovered plant alkaloid on human lung cancer cells. This study integrates which two branches?
items.e: Evaluating drug action on cells merges pharmacology (drug actions) with cell biology (cellular structure/pathology).

items.q: Which bio-element is directly required to synthesize peptide bonds in all structural and enzymatic proteins?
items.e: Nitrogen is an essential component of the amino group (-NH2) in all amino acids that form peptide bonds.

items.q: Why is Brassica campestris classified as a multicellular organism rather than a colonial organism?
o: Its cells show specialized division of labor into distinct tissues and organs
items.e: Multicellularity requires specialized differentiation of cells into distinct tissues and organs performing interdependent functions.

items.q: Which Muslim scientist authored 'Al-Tasrif' and invented more than 200 surgical tools?
items.e: Al-Zahrawi (Albucasis) was the great pioneer of surgery who authored 'Al-Tasrif'.

items.q: A patient suffering from an inherited genetic blood disorder visits a hematologist. Which field explains the transmission of this disorder from parents?
items.e: Genetics is the science of heredity and transmission of genes and genetic disorders across generations.

items.q: Which of the following kingdoms contains multicellular absorptive heterotrophs with cell walls of chitin?
items.e: Fungi are defined by absorptive heterotrophy and cell walls constructed of chitin.

items.q: The study of the distribution of species across different geographical regions of the world is known as:
items.e: Biogeography investigates where organisms live and why they are distributed that way.

items.q: What is the biological significance of water being mentioned as the basis of life in Surah Al-Anbiyah Ayah 30?
o: Protoplasm is composed of 70% to 90% water and all biochemical reactions require an aqueous medium
items.e: Cellular protoplasm is predominantly aqueous, providing the essential solvent for all enzymatic and metabolic reactions.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT an organ of the vegetative shoot system of Brassica campestris?
items.e: Flower is the sexual reproductive organ, not a vegetative organ.

items.q: A researcher notes: 'The leaves of plants grown in nitrogen-deficient soil turned pale yellow with an average chlorophyll content of 0.4 mg/g.' This statement contains:
items.e: 'Pale yellow' is qualitative (descriptive); '0.4 mg/g' is quantitative (measurable numerical data).

items.q: Why must a hypothesis always be formulated before carrying out deductive reasoning?
o: Deductions are logical consequences inferred directly from the hypothesis
items.e: Deductions use 'If-Then' conditional logic to predict consequences assuming the hypothesis is true.

items.q: An agricultural company claims fertilizer X increases wheat yield. To test this scientifically, what must the control plot receive?
o: Same soil, water, and sunlight, but ZERO fertilizer X
items.e: A control group must be identical in all abiotic factors except the test fertilizer.

items.q: What biological adaptation explains why female mosquitoes require animal blood meals while male mosquitoes do not?
o: Females require blood proteins for the maturation of their eggs
items.e: Female mosquitoes need concentrated animal proteins and iron to develop fertile eggs.

items.q: If Ronald Ross found that 28 out of 40 sparrows bitten by Culex developed malaria, how many would contract malaria in a flock of 200 sparrows under identical conditions?
Which step of the biological method ensures that scientific findings become public and open to global verification?
o: Reporting of results in scientific literature
items.e: Publishing in peer-reviewed scientific journals allows the international community to scrutinize and replicate experiments.

items.q: Why is Mendel's formulation of inheritance called a 'Law' while Darwin's concept of natural selection is called a 'Theory'?
o: Mendel used mathematics while Darwin did not
Mendel's law is a uniform mathematical generalization of allele segregation, whereas natural selection is a broad explanatory framework
items.e: Laws are concise, uniform, invariant statements of natural phenomena; theories are broad explanatory systems.

items.q: If a biologist observes that malarial patients have chills every 48 hours, which stage of the biological method is this?
items.e: Noting the recurring pattern of symptoms is an observation.

items.q: In an experiment testing drug efficacy, the subjects who receive a harmless sugar pill (placebo) constitute the:
items.e: The placebo group provides the baseline control to isolate psychological bias from pharmacological action.

items.q: Which of the following statements represents an 'If-Then' deduction?
o: If Plasmodium causes malaria, then all malarial patients should harbor Plasmodium in their blood
Malaria is common in marshy areas
items.e: An 'If-Then' statement logically derives a predicted outcome from a proposed hypothesis.

items.q: Why is the biological species concept defined by the ability to produce 'fertile' offspring rather than merely offspring?
o: Because hybridization between different species (e.g. horse and donkey producing an infertile mule) demonstrates reproductive isolation between distinct species
Because fertile offspring are always larger
Because plants do not reproduce sexually
items.e: Fertility of offspring ensures gene flow within the same species. Hybrids like mules are sterile, proving horse and donkey are distinct species.

items.q: Which criterion was used by Robert Whittaker to place Fungi into a separate kingdom distinct from Kingdom Plantae?
o: Fungi are absorptive heterotrophs with cell walls composed of chitin, lacking chlorophyll
items.e: Fungi possess chitinous walls and absorptive heterotrophic nutrition, contrasting with cellulose autotrophs.

items.q: A newly discovered micro-organism has naked DNA in a nucleoid and a peptidoglycan cell wall. In which kingdom should it be classified?
items.e: Naked DNA without nuclear membrane and peptidoglycan walls are diagnostic traits of Kingdom Monera.

items.q: Why are viruses considered borderline entities between living organisms and non-living matter?
o: They possess genetic material (DNA/RNA) and reproduce inside host cells, but can be crystallized and lack independent metabolism
items.e: Viruses exhibit replication and genetics inside hosts (living) but lack cytoplasm and form crystals (non-living).

items.q: Which endangered animal species of Pakistan is protected in the Sukkur-Guddu riverine barrage corridor?
items.e: The blind Indus River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica minor) inhabits the Indus River protected reserves.

items.q: In taxonomic hierarchy, two organisms belonging to the same Order must also belong to the same:
items.e: Taxonomic hierarchy is inclusive: organisms sharing a lower taxon (Order) necessarily share all higher taxa (Class, Phylum, Kingdom).

items.q: How does large-scale Deforestation directly accelerate the extinction of terrestrial wildlife?
o: It destroys natural habitats, disrupts food webs, and causes canopy fragmentation
items.e: Forests provide shelter, microclimates, and food webs; clear-cutting leaves species without nesting and foraging habitats.

items.q: Organisms that are unicellular eukaryotes exhibiting both autotrophic photosynthesis in light and heterotrophic ingestion in darkness are classified in:
items.e: Euglena is a protist possessing flagella and chloroplasts, displaying mixotrophic nutrition.

items.q: What is the primary conservation objective of community-managed trophy hunting programs in northern Pakistan?
o: To generate substantial revenue for local communities from permits, incentivizing them to protect Markhor from illegal poaching
items.e: Revenue sharing (80% to local villagers) transforms former poachers into active conservation guardians.

items.q: A student measures an animal cell under 400X magnification. If the cell measures 20 mm on the eyepiece reticle, what is its actual physical size?
items.e: Actual Size = Image Size / Magnification = 20 mm / 400 = 0.05 mm = 50 µm.

items.q: Which cellular organelle possesses its own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, supporting the endosymbiotic theory?
items.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have circular DNA and 70S ribosomes resembling prokaryotes.

items.q: What happens to human erythrocytes when placed in an isotonic 0.9% NaCl saline solution?
o: There is no net movement of water; cells retain normal biconcave shape
items.e: In an isotonic medium, water enters and leaves at equal rates, maintaining cell volume.

items.q: The transport of glucose into mammalian intestinal epithelial cells against its concentration gradient coupled with Na+ ions is an example of:
items.e: Moving molecules against their concentration gradient using ion-gradient energy is secondary active transport.

items.q: Which tissue consists of chondrocytes embedded in a firm, flexible rubbery matrix containing collagen fibers?
items.e: Cartilage is an elastic connective tissue composed of chondrocytes within a chondroitin matrix.

items.q: If a plant cell has a water potential of -0.4 MPa and is placed in a solution of -0.8 MPa, water will:
o: Move out of the cell causing plasmolysis
items.e: Water moves from higher water potential (-0.4 MPa) to lower water potential (-0.8 MPa), exiting the cell.

items.q: Which cellular junction in cardiac muscle tissue permits direct ionic communication between adjacent cells?
items.e: Intercalated discs contain gap junctions allowing rapid electrical transmission across myocardium.

items.q: Which organelle contains acid hydrolases capable of digesting worn-out cellular organelles (autophagy)?
items.e: Lysosomes contain acidic digestive enzymes for autophagy and cellular waste breakdown.

items.q: How does the presence of a secondary cell wall in sclerenchyma cells affect the cell's viability at maturity?
o: It thickens with impermeable lignin, causing the cell protoplast to die
It converts the cell into a chloroplast
items.e: Lignified secondary walls prevent nutrient exchange, causing sclerenchyma cells to die at functional maturity.

items.q: Why cannot an elephant be made of a single gigantic cell measuring several meters across?
o: Its surface area-to-volume ratio would be far too low to support metabolic diffusion
DNA cannot replicate in large sizes
items.e: Massive volume creates an impossibly small relative surface area, choking diffusion of nutrients and wastes.

items.q: If a cell is treated with a chemical that inhibits the polymerization of tubulin dimers into microtubules, which mitotic phase will be blocked first?
items.e: Tubulin builds the mitotic spindle; without functional microtubules, spindle fibers cannot form or align chromosomes in metaphase.

items.q: A cell in G1 phase contains 10 picograms of DNA. How much DNA will be present in the same cell at G2 phase and at the end of Telophase?
o: 10 pg in G2 and 5 pg in Telophase
20 pg in G2 and 10 pg in each daughter nucleus
10 pg in G2 and 20 pg in Telophase
40 pg in G2 and 20 pg in Telophase
items.e: DNA duplicates during S phase (10 pg ➔ 20 pg in G2). Mitotic division partitions the 20 pg equally into two daughter nuclei (10 pg each).

items.q: Why does Anaphase-I of meiosis differ fundamentally from Anaphase of mitosis?
o: Chromosomes do not move in meiosis
In Anaphase-I, homologous pairs separate while centromeres remain intact, whereas in mitotic anaphase centromeres split
Spindle fibers do not shorten in mitosis
items.e: In Anaphase-I, sister chromatids remain joined at their common centromere; only homologous pairs pull apart.

items.q: Which of the following occurs during necrosis but NOT during apoptosis?
o: Rupture of plasma membrane and inflammatory response
items.e: Membrane lysis and acute inflammation are hallmarks of necrosis; apoptotic membranes remain intact.

items.q: Human liver cells that normally do not divide but retain the potential to proliferate when liver tissue is surgically resected reside in:
items.e: Liver hepatocytes enter semi-permanent G0 and re-enter the cell cycle upon regenerative signaling.

items.q: Independent assortment of maternal and paternal chromosomes occurs during which phase of meiosis?
items.e: Random orientation and segregation of bivalents at the equator in Metaphase-I/Anaphase-I generates independent assortment.

items.q: In a human undergoing gametogenesis, a non-disjunction event where chromosome 21 fails to separate during Anaphase-I produces gametes with:
items.e: Non-disjunction sends both homologues to one pole (n+1 = 24) and none to the other (n-1 = 22), causing Down Syndrome.

items.q: What is the primary evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction?
o: It generates genetic variation via crossing over and random fertilization, aiding survival in fluctuating environments
It eliminates the need for meiosis
items.e: Sexual reproduction generates recombinant diversity, allowing populations to adapt to parasites and ecological changes.

items.q: Which structure forms the cell plate in dividing plant cells?
items.e: Golgi vesicles fuse along the phragmoplast to lay down the pectins and cellulose of the cell plate.

items.q: At which cell cycle checkpoint does the cell confirm that all kinetochores are properly attached to spindle fibers?
items.e: The M-checkpoint during metaphase delays anaphase onset until every kinetochore is bioriented.

items.q: Why does boiled saliva fail to digest starch into maltose?
o: Starch turns into glycogen upon boiling
Boiling denatures salivary amylase by destroying its tertiary structure
Boiling removes all water from saliva
Boiling converts amylase into an inorganic salt
items.e: Boiling causes irreversible thermal denaturation of amylase's active site.

items.q: If the optimum pH of an enzyme is 8.0, what will happen to its activity if the pH is lowered to 2.0?
o: The enzyme will lose its activity and become denatured
The enzyme will turn into pepsin
items.e: A massive pH shift from 8.0 to 2.0 alters active site ionization and causes denaturation.

items.q: A reaction has reached Vmax at a substrate concentration of 50 mM. How can the researcher further increase the reaction rate?
items.e: At Vmax, the enzyme is saturated; providing additional enzyme molecules provides new active sites, increasing rate.

items.q: Which of the following molecules acts as a coenzyme derived from Vitamin B3 (Niacin)?
items.e: NAD+ is a vital metabolic coenzyme synthesized from vitamin B3 (niacin).

items.q: What distinguishes a Prosthetic Group from a typical Coenzyme?
o: A prosthetic group is composed of lipids
A prosthetic group is permanently and covalently bonded to the enzyme protein
A prosthetic group acts only at 100°C
items.e: Prosthetic groups are tightly, covalently attached to the apoenzyme, whereas coenzymes bind loosely.

items.q: In an exergonic catabolic reaction, how does the potential energy of the products compare with the reactants?
o: Products have higher potential energy than reactants
Products have lower potential energy than reactants, with energy released
Energy of products is always zero
items.e: Catabolic reactions release free energy; therefore, products possess lower potential energy than reactants.

items.q: Why is the Induced Fit Model preferred over the Lock and Key Model in modern biochemistry?
o: Because enzymes are made of metal
Because X-ray crystallography proves that active sites are dynamic and undergo conformational shifts upon substrate binding
Because locks do not exist in cells
Because all enzymes act on all substrates
items.e: Structural biology confirms that active sites flex and conform snugly around substrates during catalysis.

items.q: Which enzyme is clinically added to dairy milk to produce lactose-free products for lactose-intolerant patients?
items.e: Lactase hydrolyzes milk lactose disaccharide into absorbable glucose and galactose.

items.q: Competitive inhibitors decrease the rate of enzyme reactions by:
o: Binding directly to the active site because they resemble the substrate structure
items.e: Competitive inhibitors mimic substrate geometry and compete for occupancy of the active site.

items.q: What is the function of the enzyme Rennin in the abomasum of infant ruminants and in commercial cheese making?
o: Curdle and coagulate soluble milk protein casein into insoluble paracaseinate
items.e: Rennin curdles milk casein, precipitating it into cheese curd.

items.q: If a plant is illuminated exclusively with pure green monochromatic light, what will happen to its photosynthetic rate?
o: It will drop to near zero because green light is reflected, not absorbed
It will double the production of glucose
items.e: Chlorophyll pigments reflect green wavelengths and absorb blue and red; green light alone cannot drive photosynthesis.

items.q: How many ATP molecules are produced from the complete aerobic oxidation of two molecules of glucose in human cardiac myocytes?
items.e: One glucose yields 36 net ATP in eukaryotes; two glucose molecules yield 36 × 2 = 72 net ATP.

items.q: Why does bread dough rise and become soft and spongy when baker's yeast (Saccharomyces) is added?
o: Yeast performs alcoholic fermentation, releasing CO2 bubbles that get trapped in the gluten dough matrix
items.e: Anaerobic fermentation by yeast produces CO2 gas, which expands when baked, creating spongy pores.

items.q: In which part of the chloroplast does the photolysis (light splitting) of water molecules take place?
items.e: The oxygen-evolving complex associated with Photosystem-II is located on the luminal side of the thylakoid membrane.

items.q: Cyanide is a lethal poison that blocks cytochrome oxidase in the electron transport chain. What is the immediate biochemical effect?
o: ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation stops, causing rapid cell death
items.e: Blocking the respiratory chain stops proton pumping and ATP synthesis, causing cellular asphyxiation.

items.q: The primary photosynthetic enzyme that fixes CO2 onto RuBP in the Calvin cycle is:
items.e: Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO) catalyzes the initial carbon-fixing step.

items.q: What is the primary role of accessory pigments like Carotenoids in photosynthetic leaves?
o: They absorb intermediate light wavelengths and protect chlorophyll from photo-oxidative damage
items.e: Carotenoids expand the absorption spectrum and dissipate excessive light energy, shielding chlorophyll from damage.

items.q: Which of the following processes occurs in both Aerobic Respiration and Anaerobic Fermentation?
items.e: Glycolysis is the universal evolutionary pathway common to both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

items.q: During chemiosmosis in mitochondria, protons (H+) are pumped across the inner membrane into the:
items.e: Respiratory complexes pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, establishing an electrochemical gradient.

items.q: Why is cellular respiration considered an exergonic catabolic process?
o: It breaks down high-energy covalent bonds in organic food, releasing free energy stored in ATP
items.e: Catabolism involves breaking bonds to liberate chemical energy (exergonic).

items.q: Why are fatty acids and glycerol absorbed into lacteals rather than blood capillaries in the intestinal villi?
o: They form large lipid-protein complexes called chylomicrons, which are too large to penetrate blood capillary pores
items.e: Chylomicrons (100–500 nm) are too large for capillary fenestrations and enter the more permeable lacteals.

items.q: A patient with bleeding gums and slow-healing surgical wounds is likely suffering from a deficiency of:
items.e: Vitamin C is essential for collagen synthesis; its deficiency causes scurvy (fragile capillaries, bleeding gums).

items.q: What is the biological consequence of surgical removal of the Gallbladder (Cholecystectomy)?
o: Bile drips continuously and slowly into the duodenum, requiring the patient to reduce intake of fatty meals
items.e: The liver still produces bile, but without the storage gallbladder, concentrated bile cannot be surged for fatty meals.

items.q: Which mineral deficiency is directly responsible for Nutritional Goiter in human populations living in mountainous regions?
items.e: Iodine is required to synthesize thyroxine; deficiency leads to compensatory thyroid enlargement (goiter).

items.q: Why does consuming excessive dietary fiber prevent the development of Constipation?
o: Insoluble cellulose holds water, softens stool, and adds bulk to stimulate intestinal peristalsis
items.e: Dietary fiber retains moisture, creating soft bulky stools that trigger rhythmic peristaltic reflexes.

items.q: A blood sample from the Hepatic Portal Vein after a carbohydrate meal contains high glucose, while blood leaving the Hepatic Vein is normal (90 mg/dL). What occurred?
o: The liver excreted the glucose in bile
The liver stored excess glucose as glycogen under the influence of insulin
The kidneys filtered out the glucose
items.e: The liver buffers blood glucose by storing postprandial glucose excess as glycogen.

items.q: Why is Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) therapy supplemented with glucose rather than pure saline?
o: Sodium ions are co-transported across the intestinal epithelium coupled with glucose (SGLT-1 co-transporter)
items.e: The sodium-glucose co-transporter requires glucose to efficiently drag sodium and water into epithelial cells.

items.q: Which enzyme converts inactive trypsinogen into active trypsin in the duodenum?
items.e: Enterokinase secreted by duodenal mucosa activates pancreatic trypsinogen into trypsin.

items.q: If a plant soil lacks both nitrogen and magnesium, what severe symptom will manifest first on mature leaves?
items.e: Both nitrogen and magnesium are structural constituents of chlorophyll; deficiency causes severe chlorosis.

items.q: Which vitamin deficiency causes Rickets (soft, curved leg bones) in growing children?
items.e: Vitamin D is essential for intestinal calcium absorption and bone mineralization; deficiency causes rickets.

items.q: A potometer is an experimental laboratory apparatus specifically designed to measure:
o: Rate of water absorption proportional to transpiration
items.e: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot, which closely approximates transpiration rate.

items.q: Why does the rate of transpiration decrease drastically in still, highly humid air on a rainy day?
o: The water vapor concentration gradient between the internal leaf air spaces and external atmosphere is eliminated
items.e: Diffusion requires a concentration gradient; humid air saturates external vapor, halting net outward diffusion.

items.q: If a patient with Blood Group B receives a transfusion of Blood Group A red blood cells, what catastrophic immunological event occurs?
o: Recipient's Anti-A antibodies bind and agglutinate donor's Antigen A red cells, causing fatal hemolysis
Donor blood converts recipient blood into group O
Blood pressure drops to zero immediately with no clumping
items.e: Type B plasma harbors Anti-A antibodies, which destroy incoming Type A erythrocytes (acute hemolytic transfusion reaction).

items.q: In which cardiovascular condition is an artery grafted to bypass an atheromatous blockage in a coronary vessel?
items.e: CABG surgery grafts a harvest vessel to detour blood flow around coronary occlusions.

items.q: What prevents backflow of blood from the ventricles into the atria during ventricular systole?
items.e: The AV valves close tightly during ventricular contraction to prevent blood regurgitation into the atria.

items.q: Which type of white blood cell differentiates into large phagocytic Macrophages in inflamed body tissues?
items.e: Circulating blood monocytes migrate into infected tissues and mature into voracious macrophages.

items.q: Why do veins possess internal pocket-like semilunar valves while arteries do not?
o: Blood in veins flows under low pressure and valves prevent gravity from causing backward blood pooling
items.e: Low venous pressure requires one-way valves to assist venous return against gravitational pull.

items.q: Which blood component maintains colloidal plasma osmotic pressure, preventing edema in human tissues?
items.e: Serum albumin exerts oncotic pressure, retaining water inside the intravascular compartment.

items.q: The inherited blood disorder caused by defective beta-globin chain synthesis resulting in frequent hemolytic anemia is:
items.e: Beta-thalassemia is an autosomal recessive disorder impairing hemoglobin synthesis.

items.q: In an experiment, ringing or girdling a woody stem by removing a ring of outer bark down to the xylem causes:
o: Accumulation of organic sugars and swelling of bark immediately above the ring, because phloem was severed
items.e: Girdling removes phloem (in bark) while leaving xylem intact; downward transport of sugars stops, swelling the upper bark.

items.q: How the understanding of physics can help the biologist?
items.a: Biophysics applies the laws and instrumentation of physics to biological systems. Examples: 1. Light Absorption in Photosynthesis: Chlorophyll absorbs specific wavelengths of electromagnetic light energy following physical optics and quantum energy transfer. 2. Biomechanics of Movement: The lever mechanics of human bones and joints obey physical principles of levers, moments, and torque.

items.q: How the understanding of biology can be improved through knowledge of geography, chemistry and statistics? Give examples.
items.a: Biology relies intimately on allied physical and mathematical disciplines: 1. Biogeography (Linkage with Geography): • Explains the distribution of plant and animal species across Earth's continents, biomes, and climatic belts. • Example: Why polar bears possess thick blubber and white insulating fur exclusively in Arctic ice sheets, or why xerophytic cacti flourish in arid desert sand dunes. 2. Biochemistry (Linkage with Chemistry): • Explores the chemical composition, molecular structures, and chemical reactions within living cells. • Example: Digestion of starch into glucose via enzymatic hydrolysis, ATP generation during cellular respiration (glycolysis and citric acid cycle), and carbon fixation during photosynthesis. 3. Biostatistics / Biometry (Linkage with Mathematics & Statistics): • Employs statistical formulas to design clinical trials, analyze biological variance, and calculate averages, ratios, and standard deviations. • Example: Determining the statistical efficacy of a newly engineered malaria vaccine across experimental and control groups.

items.q: Explain the role of bio elements for living organisms.
items.a: Out of 92 naturally occurring elements, 16 are essential for life and termed Bio-elements: 1. Major Bio-elements (6 elements make up 99% of body mass): • Oxygen (65%): Essential for aerobic respiration and constituent of water and organic molecules. • Carbon (18%): The structural backbone of all organic biomolecules (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, DNA). • Hydrogen (10%): Constituent of water and carrier of electrons/protons in metabolic redox reactions. • Nitrogen (3%): Essential building block of all amino acids, proteins, nucleotides, and RNA/DNA. • Calcium (2%): Key mineral in bone and teeth formation, muscle contraction, and blood clotting. • Phosphorus (1%): Integral component of nucleic acids, cell membrane phospholipids, and ATP energy currency. 2. Trace Bio-elements (10 elements make up remaining 1%): • Potassium (K) & Sodium (Na): Crucial for nerve impulse conduction and osmoregulation. • Iron (Fe): Central cofactor in hemoglobin for oxygen transport in blood. • Magnesium (Mg): Central atom in chlorophyll and enzyme activator. • Chlorine (Cl), Sulfur (S), Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn), Manganese (Mn), and Iodine (I): Vital enzymatic cofactors and thyroid hormone synthesis.

items.q: Enlist the various levels of biological organization and explain it with example.
items.a: Living matter is organized in ascending hierarchical complexity: 1. Subatomic and Atomic Level: • Protons, neutrons, and electrons form atoms of chemical elements. Six major bio-elements (C, H, O, N, Ca, P) constitute 99% of protoplasm. 2. Molecular Level: • Atoms bond to form biomolecules: Micromolecules (glucose, water, amino acids) and Macromolecules (proteins, glycogen, nucleic acids). 3. Organelle and Cell Level: • Biomolecules assemble into functional subcellular compartments called organelles (mitochondria, chloroplasts, Golgi apparatus). The cell is the fundamental unit of life. 4. Tissue Level: • Groups of similar cells specialized for a cooperative function form tissues (e.g., xylem and phloem in plants; muscular and nervous tissue in animals). 5. Organ and Organ System Level: • Multiple tissues combine to form an organ (e.g., stomach with muscular and epithelial tissues). Multiple organs form an organ system (e.g., digestive system comprising mouth, stomach, pancreas, and intestines). 6. Individual Organism Level: • Coordinated organ systems function collaboratively to create an independent living individual (e.g., human, Mustard plant).

items.a: (a) Comparison between Compound and Mixture: 1. Formation: Compound is formed by chemical combination of constituent elements with bond formation. Mixture is formed by simple physical mixing without chemical bonds. 2. Properties: In a compound, elements lose their original properties and form entirely new substances (e.g. H2 and O2 gases form liquid H2O). In a mixture, components retain their original properties (e.g. sugar dissolved in water retains sweetness). 3. Composition: Compound has a strict, fixed ratio by mass (e.g. H2O is always 2:16 or 1:8 by mass). Mixture has variable composition in any proportion. 4. Separation: Compounds cannot be separated by physical methods; they require chemical decomposition. Mixtures can be separated by physical methods (filtration, distillation, magnet, evaporation). 5. Representation: Compounds have a definite chemical formula (e.g. NaCl, CaCO3). Mixtures have no chemical formula. 6. Melting/Boiling Point: Compounds have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points. Mixtures do not have sharp melting points. Examples: Compounds = Water (H2O), Sodium Chloride (NaCl), Carbon Dioxide (CO2). Mixtures = Air, Brass alloy, Sand in water, Petroleum. (b) Classification of Molecules: 1. Classification Based on Atomicity (Number of Atoms): • Monoatomic molecules: Helium (He), Argon (Ar), Neon (Ne). • Diatomic molecules: Hydrogen (H2), Oxygen (O2), Carbo

items.a: 1. Atomic Number (Z): The total number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom of that element. It determines the chemical identity and position of the element in the periodic table.
items.e: 2. Mass Number (A): The total sum of protons and neutrons (nucleons) present inside the nucleus (A = Z + N). Difference: Atomic number counts only protons (Z), whereas mass number counts both protons and neutrons (A = Z + N). Atomic number is unique and identical for all isotopes of an element, while mass number varies among isotopes.

items.a: (a) Empirical Formula: 1. Definition: The empirical formula of a chemical compound is the simplest chemical formula that shows the lowest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element present in the compound. 2. Characteristics: • It represents the simplest atomic composition but not necessarily the actual total number of atoms. • For ionic compounds, the empirical formula is identical to the formula unit (e.g. NaCl, CaCl2). 3. Examples: • Benzene: Molecular formula is C6H6. The ratio of C:H is 6:6, which simplifies to 1:1. Hence, empirical formula = CH. • Glucose: Molecular formula is C6H12O6. The ratio of C:H:O is 6:12:6, which simplifies to 1:2:1. Hence, empirical formula = CH2O. • Hydrogen Peroxide: Molecular formula is H2O2. Ratio of H:O is 2:2 → 1:1. Hence, empirical formula = HO. (b) Molecular Formula: 1. Definition: The molecular formula is the chemical formula that expresses the actual number of atoms of each element present in one molecule of a compound. 2. Mathematical Relationship with Empirical Formula: • Molecular Formula = n × (Empirical Formula) • Where 'n' is an integer (n = 1, 2, 3, 4...) calculated as: n = Molar Mass of Compound / Empirical Formula Mass 3. Examples: • Benzene: Empirical formula = CH (mass = 12 + 1 = 13). Molecular mass = 78 amu. n = 78 / 13 = 6. Molecular formula = 6 × (CH) = C6H6. • Glucose: Empirical formula = CH2O (mass = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30).

items.a: (a) Molecular Mass vs Formula Mass: 1. Molecular Mass: The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms present in one discrete molecule of a covalent substance (e.g. H2O, CH4, C6H6). 2. Formula Mass: The sum of the atomic masses of all the ions present in one representative formula unit of an ionic crystal lattice (e.g. NaCl, AlCl3, Fe2O3). Difference: Molecular mass applies strictly to molecular/covalent compounds existing as individual discrete molecules. Formula mass applies to ionic compounds that exist as infinite 3D crystalline arrays without separate individual molecules. (b) Step-by-Step Calculations: (i) Benzene (C6H6) — Molecular Mass: • 6 C = 6 × 12.0 amu = 72.0 amu • 6 H = 6 × 1.0 amu = 6.0 amu • Molecular Mass = 72.0 + 6.0 = 78.0 amu (ii) Ethane gas (C2H6) — Molecular Mass: • 2 C = 2 × 12.0 amu = 24.0 amu • 6 H = 6 × 1.0 amu = 6.0 amu • Molecular Mass = 24.0 + 6.0 = 30.0 amu (iii) Aluminum chloride (AlCl3) — Formula Mass: • 1 Al = 1 × 27.0 amu = 27.0 amu • 3 Cl = 3 × 35.5 amu = 106.5 amu • Formula Mass = 27.0 + 106.5 = 133.5 amu (iv) Iron oxide (Fe2O3) — Formula Mass: • 2 Fe = 2 × 56.0 amu = 112.0 amu • 3 O = 3 × 16.0 amu = 48.0 amu • Formula Mass = 112.0 + 48.0 = 160.0 amu

items.a: 1. Avogadro's Number (NA): • Definition: Avogadro's number is defined as the exact number of particles (atoms, molecules, ions, or formula units) present in exactly one mole of any pure chemical substance. • Numerical Value: NA = 6.023 × 10^23 particles. • Significance: Since individual atoms and molecules are sub-microscopic and cannot be counted individually, Avogadro's number serves as the fundamental counting bridge connecting macroscopic laboratory masses (grams) to microscopic particle quantities. 2. The Mole Concept (mol): • Qualitative Definition: A mole is the amount of a substance that contains exactly 6.023 × 10^23 representative particles of that substance. • Quantitative Definition: The atomic mass, molecular mass, or formula mass of any chemical substance expressed in grams is termed as one mole (or molar mass). 3. Comprehensive Illustrative Examples: • Gram Atomic Mass: Atomic mass of Carbon = 12 amu → 12.0 g of Carbon = 1 mole of C = 6.023 × 10^23 carbon atoms. • Gram Molecular Mass: Molecular mass of Water (H2O) = 18 amu → 18.0 g of Water = 1 mole of H2O = 6.023 × 10^23 water molecules. • Gram Formula Mass: Formula mass of Sodium Chloride (NaCl) = 58.5 amu → 58.5 g of NaCl = 1 mole of NaCl = 6.023 × 10^23 NaCl formula units (containing 6.023 × 10^23 Na+ ions and 6.023 × 10^23 Cl- ions). 4. items.a: 1. Experimental Setup: In 1911, Lord Rutherford bombarded a thin gold foil (thickness 0.00004 cm) with ~20,000 high-energy alpha particles (^4_2 He^2+) emitted from a radioactive Polonium source. A circular fluorescent Zinc Sulphide (ZnS) screen detected particle deflections. 2. Experimental Observations: • Majority (~19,990 out of 20,000) passed straight through the gold foil with zero deflection. • A small fraction (~8 particles) suffered small-angle deflections. • A very rare fraction (~2 particles) bounced straight back along their original trajectory. 3. Rutherford's Deductions & Atomic Model Postulates: • Central Nucleus: An extremely small, dense, positively charged core called the 'nucleus' is located at the center of the atom. • Empty Volume: Since almost all alpha particles passed undeflected, most of the volume of an atom is empty space. • Planetary Electrons: Negatively charged electrons revolve around the nucleus at high speeds, resembling planets orbiting the sun. • Electrical Neutrality: The total positive charge of nuclear protons exactly equals the total negative charge of orbital electrons. • Mass Concentration: The entire mass and positive charge of the atom are concentrated in the nucleus.

items.a: In 1913, Neil Bohr formulated his quantum atomic model based on Max Planck's quantum theory of radiation to overcome Rutherford's instability defects: 1. Fixed Quantized Orbits: Electrons revolve around the nucleus only in specific, fixed circular paths called stationary shells or energy levels (n = 1, 2, 3... or K, L, M, N). 2. Energy Proportional to Radius: The energy of an electron in an orbit is directly proportional to its distance from the nucleus. K-shell has minimum energy; energy increases outward. 3. Non-Radiating Stationary States: As long as an electron remains in a particular orbit, it neither radiates nor absorbs energy. Its energy remains strictly constant. 4. Energy Absorption and Emission: Energy is absorbed only when an electron jumps from a lower energy orbit (E1) to a higher energy orbit (E2), and energy is emitted (as a photon) when it falls from a higher orbit (E2) to a lower orbit (E1): ΔE = E2 - E1 = hν (where h = 6.6262 × 10^-34 J·s) 5. Quantized Angular Momentum: An electron can revolve only in those orbits where its orbital angular momentum (mvr) is an integral multiple of h / 2π: mvr = nh / 2π (where n = 1, 2, 3, 4...) 6. Stability Explanation: Because angular momentum and orbits are quantized, electrons cannot spiral continuously into the nucleus, ensuring atomic stability and explaining discrete line spectra.

items.a: An atom is considered electrically neutral because: 1. It contains an equal number of positively charged protons inside the nucleus and negatively charged electrons revolving in the shells outside the nucleus (Number of Protons = Number of Electrons). 2. The positive electrical charge on one proton (+1.6022 × 10^-19 C) is exactly equal in magnitude to the negative charge on one electron (-1.6022 × 10^-19 C). 3. Neutrons carry zero charge (neutral). Thus, the opposite charges completely balance and cancel each other out, resulting in a net electrical charge of zero.

Lithium (Li, Z = 3, 3 electrons): • Energy Levels: K-shell = 2 electrons, L-shell = 1 electron • Sub-energy Levels: 1s^2 2s^1 4. Beryllium (Be, Z = 4, 4 electrons): • Energy Levels: K-shell = 2 electrons, L-shell = 2 electrons • Sub-energy Levels: 1s^2 2s^2

items.a: 1. Why chemical properties are the SAME: Chemical properties of an element depend entirely on the number of valence electrons and electronic configuration. items.a: Comparison between Mendeleev's and Modern Periodic Table: 1. Basis of Arrangement: • Mendeleev's Table (1869): Elements were arranged in increasing order of their Atomic Masses (Atomic Weights). • Modern Table (Moseley, 1913): Elements are arranged in increasing order of their Atomic Numbers (Z). 2. Periodic Law: • Mendeleev: Properties are periodic functions of atomic masses. • Modern: Properties are periodic functions of atomic numbers. 3. Position of Isotopes: • Mendeleev: Could not explain where isotopes should be placed (since isotopes have different atomic masses but same chemical properties). • Modern: All isotopes of an element have the identical atomic number, so they occupy the same position naturally. 4. Anomalous Pairs (Irregular Mass Orders): • Mendeleev: Certain elements with higher atomic masses had to be placed before lower mass elements to maintain chemical groupings (e.g. Ar-40 before K-39, Te-128 before I-127, Co-59 before Ni-58.7). • Modern: When arranged by atomic number (Ar=18, K=19; Co=27, Ni=28; Te=52, I=53), all mass anomalies vanish completely. 5. Electronic Structure & Subshell Blocks: • Mendeleev: Had no connection to electronic configurations. • Modern: Clearly divided into s, p, d, and f blocks reflecting valence electron subshells.

items.a: (a) Differentiation: 1. Atomic Radius (r): The distance between the center of the nucleus and the outermost valence shell of an isolated single atom. Expressed in pm or Å. 2. Covalent Radius: Exactly one-half of the distance between the nuclei of two identical atoms bonded together in a homonuclear single covalent bond (r = d / 2, e.g. for Cl2 bond length 199 pm → r = 99.5 or 100 pm). (b) Periodic Trends: 1. Trend Across a Period (Left to Right): Atomic radius DECREASES across a period from alkali metals to halogens. • Reason: Nuclear charge (Z) increases by +1 unit with each successive element while additional electrons enter the same valence shell. The increased positive pull of the nucleus draws the electron cloud closer, shrinking the atomic volume. 2. Trend Down a Group (Top to Bottom): Atomic radius INCREASES down a group. • Reason: An entire new principal electron shell (n) is added with each step down a group. The increased physical distance and the screening effect of inner core electron shells reduce the effective nuclear pull, expanding atomic size.

items.a: 1. Definition of Shielding Effect (Screening Effect): The phenomenon in which inner core electron shells repel the outer valence electrons and screen them from the full positive attractive pull of the nucleus is called the Shielding Effect. 2. Impact of Shielding Effect on Periodic Properties: • On Ionization Energy (IE): Inversely proportional. Greater shielding down a group weakens nuclear attraction on valence electrons, causing Ionization Energy to DECREASE. • On Electron Affinity (EA): Inversely proportional. Greater shielding reduces the nucleus's ability to attract an incoming extra electron, causing Electron Affinity to DECREASE (become less negative). • On Electronegativity (EN): Inversely proportional. Increased shielding screens the positive nucleus from attracting shared bonded electron pairs, causing Electronegativity to DECREASE. 3. Summary Trend Chart (Fig 3.9): • Down a Group: Shielding increases → IE decreases, EA decreases, EN decreases, Atomic radius increases. • Across a Period: Shielding remains constant while Nuclear Charge increases → IE increases, EA increases, EN increases, Atomic radius decreases.

items.a: 1. Definition of Electronegativity (EN): Electronegativity is the relative tendency or ability of an atom in a molecule to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a covalent bond (measured on the Linus Pauling scale from 0.7 to 4.0). 2. Most and Least Electronegative Groups: • Most Electronegative Group: Group VIIA (Halogens, Group 17). They have small atomic radii, high effective nuclear charge, and only need 1 electron to achieve noble gas stability. • Least Electronegative Group: Group IA (Alkali metals, Group 1). They have large atomic radii, low nuclear attraction, and readily lose electrons. 3. Why Fluorine (F) is Special: • Fluorine has the highest electronegativity value of ALL 118 elements (assigned exactly 4.0 on the Pauling scale). • Reason: Fluorine (Z = 9, 1s2 2s2 2p5) has the smallest atomic radius among all halogen atoms with an extremely high effective nuclear charge acting on its compact valence shell. It attracts shared electron pairs more strongly than any other element, making it an extraordinarily aggressive oxidizing agent.

items.e: Reason: In Carbon dioxide (O=C=O), the two C=O bonds are polar because oxygen is significantly more electronegative than carbon (ΔEN = 3.5 - 2.5 = 1.0). However, because CO2 has a linear molecular geometry (bond angle 180°), the two individual bond dipoles are equal in magnitude but point in exactly opposite directions, canceling each other out completely. Consequently, the net dipole moment is zero, making CO2 an overall non-polar molecule.

Mechanism of Formation: • Ionic Bond: Formed by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metallic atom (electropositive) to a non-metallic atom (electronegative). Example: Formation of Sodium Chloride (NaCl). Sodium (2,8,1) transfers its 1 valence electron to Chlorine (2,8,7), producing Na+ (2,8) and Cl- (2,8,8). Electrostatic attraction between Na+ and Cl- forms the ionic crystal. • Covalent Bond: Formed by the mutual sharing of valence electrons between two non-metallic atoms of similar or moderate electronegativity. Example: Formation of Chlorine molecule (Cl2). Each Cl atom (2,8,7) shares 1 electron with the other, forming a single shared electron pair (Cl─Cl). 2. Nature of Units: • Ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional crystalline lattices of cations and anions (no discrete molecules). • Covalent compounds exist as discrete, individual molecules. 3. Physical Properties: • Ionic compounds have high melting/boiling points and conduct electricity in molten/solution states. • Covalent compounds typically have lower melting/boiling points and are non-electrolytes. Structure and Deformation in Metals (Malleable and Ductile): • In metallic bonding, positive metal ions (kernels) are arranged in uniform layers surrounded by a continuous, mobile 'sea' of delocalized electrons. • The metallic bond is non-directional and flexible. When an external mechanical force (hammering or stretching) is applied to a metal, layers of metal ions can slide smoothly over one another into new positions without breaking the metallic bond. • As the layers slide, the mobile delocalized electrons instantly adjust and continue to maintain strong electrostatic attraction with the metal ions in their new positions. • Consequently, metals can be beaten into thin sheets (malleability) and drawn into long wires (ductility) without shattering. 2. items.a: (a) Meaning of the Term 'Polar' in Chemical Bonding: In chemical bonding, the term 'polar' refers to the uneven, asymmetrical distribution of electrical charge across a bond or molecule. When two bonded atoms have different electronegativities, the more electronegative atom pulls the shared pair of electrons closer to itself. This unequal sharing creates partial electrical charges (a dipole): a partial negative charge (δ-) on the more electronegative atom and an equal partial positive charge (δ+) on the less electronegative atom. A bond possessing such distinct positive and negative poles is called a polar bond. (b) Distinction between Polar Covalent and Non-Polar Covalent Bonds: 1. Definition: • Non-Polar Covalent Bond: Formed by equal sharing of electrons between atoms of identical or nearly identical electronegativities. • Polar Covalent Bond: Formed by unequal sharing of electrons between atoms of significantly different electronegativities. 2. Electronegativity Difference (ΔEN): • Non-Polar: ΔEN is 0.0 to 0.4 (or identical atoms). • Polar: ΔEN is 0.5 to 1.7. 3. Charge Distribution: • Non-Polar: Electron cloud is completely symmetrical; no partial electrical poles (δ+/δ-) are created. • Polar: Electron cloud is asymmetrical and shifted toward the more electronegative atom; permanent partial charges (δ+ and δ-) develop. 4. items.a: 1. Definition of Octet Rule: The octet rule (or Rule of Eight) states that atoms tend to lose, gain, or share valence electrons in order to acquire a stable electronic configuration consisting of eight electrons in their outermost valence shell, identical to the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas (Group VIIIA). 2. Noble Gas Electronic Configurations and Inherent Stability: Except for helium (He, 1s2, duplet configuration of 2 electrons), all noble gases (Neon: 2,8; Argon: 2,8,8; Krypton: 2,8,18,8; Xenon; Radon) possess completely filled outermost s and p subshells containing exactly eight valence electrons (ns2 np6). This completely filled octet represents a state of maximum electrostatic symmetry and minimum potential energy. Because their valence shells are full, noble gases do not readily gain, lose, or share electrons and remain monoatomic and chemically inert under normal conditions. 3. How Other Atoms Achieve Stability: Isolated atoms of representative elements (groups IA through VIIA) have incomplete valence shells (1 to 7 electrons). items.a: The four major types of chemical bonding are: 1. Ionic Bond: The chemical bond formed by the complete transfer of one or more electrons from a metallic atom to a non-metallic atom (e.g. NaCl). 2. Covalent Bond: The bond formed by the mutual sharing of valence electrons between two non-metallic atoms (e.g. H2, Cl2, CH4). 3. Coordinate Covalent (Dative) Bond: A covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom only (e.g. NH4+, NH3-BCl3). 4. Metallic Bond: The electrostatic attraction between positively charged metal ions and the mobile sea of delocalized electrons in a metallic lattice (e.g. Cu, Fe, Al).

items.q: Define Boyle's law and verify it experimentally.

items.a: 1. Statement of Boyle's Law: Robert Boyle (1662) formulated this fundamental gas law: 'The volume of a given mass of an ideal gas is inversely proportional to the applied pressure, provided the temperature remains constant.' 2. Mathematical Expression: V ∝ 1/P (at constant T and n) V = Kb × (1/P) => P × V = Kb (constant) For a gas changing from state 1 (P1, V1) to state 2 (P2, V2): P1V1 = P2V2 = Kb 3. Experimental Verification: • Apparatus: A gas cylinder fitted with a frictionless, airtight movable piston and weights, maintaining constant temperature (Fig. 5.4). • Procedure: a. Enclose a fixed mass of gas at an initial pressure P1 (e.g. 1 atm) and measure volume V1 (e.g. 4.0 dm^3). Product P1 × V1 = 1 × 4 = 4.0 atm·dm^3. b. Double the pressure to P2 = 2 atm by placing additional weights on the piston. The volume reduces to V2 = 2.0 dm^3. Product P2 × V2 = 2 × 2 = 4.0 atm·dm^3. c. Increase pressure to P3 = 4 atm; volume decreases to V3 = 1.0 dm^3. Product P3 × V3 = 4 × 1 = 4.0 atm·dm^3. • Conclusion: In each observation, the product P × V remains constant (Kb = 4.0), which proves and experimentally verifies Boyle's Law.

items.q: Define Charles's law and verify it graphically and diagrammatically.
items.q2: چارلس کا قانون بیان اور گراف و خاکے سے تصدیق کریں۔

items.a: 1. Statement of Charles's Law: Jacques Charles (1787) stated: 'The volume of a given mass of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (in Kelvin), provided the pressure remains constant.' 2. Mathematical Expression: V ∝ T (at constant P and n) V = Kc × T => V / T = Kc (constant) For a gas changing from state 1 (V1, T1) to state 2 (V2, T2): V1 / T1 = V2 / T2 = Kc (Note: T must always be expressed in Kelvin: K = °C + 273). 3. Graphical Verification: • If the volume 'V' of a gas is plotted against absolute temperature 'T' (in Kelvin) on a Cartesian graph at constant pressure, a straight line passing through the origin (0 K) is obtained (Fig. 5.8). • This linear relationship (isobar) confirms that volume expands in exact direct proportion to absolute temperature. 4. Diagrammatic Verification: • Consider a fixed mass of gas in a cylinder fitted with a movable piston under constant atmospheric pressure P (Fig. 5.9): - At initial temperature T1 = 300 K, gas occupies volume V1 = 2 dm^3 (V1/T1 = 2/300 = 0.0066 dm^3/K). - When heated to T2 = 600 K (doubled), the thermal kinetic energy of gas molecules increases; they strike the piston with greater force, pushing it upward until volume expands to V2 = 4 dm^3 (doubled). - Ratio V2/T2 = 4/600 = 0.0066 dm^3/K = constant Kc. • This diagrammatic demonstration verifies that volume expands proportionally with temperature

items.a: The boiling point of a liquid is directly proportional to the external atmospheric pressure. A liquid boils when its internal vapour pressure becomes equal to the external atmospheric pressure: • When atmospheric pressure increases (e.g. inside a pressure cooker), the liquid must reach a higher temperature for its vapour pressure to match external pressure; hence boiling point increases. • When atmospheric pressure decreases (e.g. at high altitudes or in vacuum distillation), vapour pressure equals external pressure at a lower temperature; hence boiling point decreases.

items.a: 1. Definition of Solids: Solids represent the state of matter in which constituent particles (atoms, ions, or molecules) are tightly packed in fixed structural arrangements by strong cohesive forces. Solids possess definite shape, definite volume, high rigidity, and incompressibility, with particles exhibiting only vibrational motion. 2. Comprehensive Distinction: • Particle Arrangement: - Crystalline: Regular, highly ordered three-dimensional repeating geometric pattern (long-range order). - Amorphous: Irregular, disordered arrangement lacking long-range repeating order. • Melting Point: - Crystalline: Sharp, precise melting point (e.g. ice melts at 0°C, NaCl melts at 801°C). - Amorphous: No sharp melting point; softens and melts gradually over a broad temperature range. • Cleavage & Geometry: - Crystalline: Cleaves smoothly along specific crystalline planes with definite interfacial angles. - Amorphous: Fractures irregularly with curved, rough surfaces (conchoidal fracture). • Heat of Fusion: - Crystalline: Possesses a definite and characteristic latent heat of fusion. - Amorphous: Lacks a definite latent heat of fusion. • Physical Nature: - Crystalline: Considered 'True solids'. - Amorphous: Considered 'Pseudo-solids' or supercooled liquids. • Examples: - Crystalline: NaCl, Diamond, Graphite, Copper sulphate (CuSO4), Ice, Naphthalene. - Amorphous: Glass, Rubber, Candle wax,

items.a: Classification with Rationale: (i) Milk ── Colloid (Liquid emulsion of butterfat globules and protein dispersed in water; shows Tyndall effect, does not settle). (ii) Hot cup of tea ── Solution (Clear homogeneous liquid solution of dissolved tea tannins and aroma compounds in water). (iii) Orange juice with pulp ── Suspension (Heterogeneous mixture with large, visible pulp particles that settle over time and are retained on filtration). (iv) Mayonnaise ── Colloid (Stable liquid emulsion of oil dispersed in vinegar/water stabilized by egg yolk lecithin). (viii) Mist ── Colloid (Liquid aerosol consisting of microscopic liquid water droplets dispersed in air). (ix) Mineral water ── Solution (Homogeneous, transparent true solution of dissolved mineral ions in water).

Solubility = [Mass of solute (g) / Mass of solvent (g)] × 100. (b) Factors Responsible for Solubility: 1. Nature of Solute and Solvent ('Like Dissolves Like'): • Polar and ionic solutes dissolve readily in polar solvents (e.g. NaCl, sugar in water) because strong electrostatic ion-dipole or dipole-dipole attractions overcome solute lattice energies. • Non-polar solutes dissolve in non-polar solvents (e.g. grease in petrol/CCl4). • Non-polar substances do not dissolve in polar water due to lack of compatible attractive forces. 2. Effect of Temperature: • Endothermic dissolution (solute absorbs heat upon dissolving, ΔH > 0): Solubility increases with temperature (e.g. KNO3, CaCl2, Pb(NO3)2). • Exothermic dissolution (solute releases heat upon dissolving, ΔH < 0): Solubility decreases with temperature (e.g. Ce2(SO4)3, Li2CO3, CaO). • Nearly constant solubility: NaCl and KBr. • Discontinuous curve: Na2SO4·10H2O transforms to anhydrous Na2SO4 at 32.4°C, where solubility reaches its peak. • Gases in liquids: Solubility of all gases decreases with increasing temperature. 3. items.a: To prove experimentally that sugar + water is a true solution and sand + water is a suspension (not a solution), perform the following two laboratory tests: 1. Filtration Test: • Sugar + Water: Pass the mixture through standard filter paper in a funnel. The entire mixture passes through cleanly into the receiving flask as a clear filtrate; no sugar residue remains on the filter paper because sugar molecules are molecularly dissolved (<1 nm). • Sand + Water: Pass the mixture through filter paper. The sand particles (>1000 nm) are completely trapped on the filter paper as residue, while clear water passes through as filtrate. 2. Settling / Stability Test: • Sugar + Water: Leave the mixture undisturbed on a laboratory bench for several days. It remains perfectly transparent and homogeneous throughout; no solute settles to the bottom. • Sand + Water: Leave the mixture undisturbed. Within seconds to minutes, all dense sand particles settle to the bottom by sedimentation, forming two distinct phases. Conclusion: These tests prove that sugar in water is a homogeneous true solution, whereas sand in water is a heterogeneous suspension.

items.a: Comprehensive Comparison between Group IA (Alkali Metals) and Group IIA (Alkaline Earth Metals): 1. Electronic Configuration & Valency: • Group IA: ns^1 configuration; lose 1 electron to form univalent M+ cations. • Group IIA: ns^2 configuration; lose 2 electrons to form divalent M2+ cations. 2. Ionization Energy & Reactivity: • Group IA: Very low 1st IE (e.g. Na = 496 kJ/mol); most reactive metals, react violently at room temperature. • Group IIA: Higher 1st & 2nd IE (e.g. Mg = 738 and 1451 kJ/mol); less reactive, often require heating. 3. Hardness, Melting & Boiling Points: • Group IA: Very soft (can be cut with a knife), low density (Na floats on water), low melting points (Na mp = 97.6°C). • Group IIA: Harder, denser (Mg = 1.74 g/cm^3), higher melting points (Mg mp = 651°C, Ca mp = 851°C). 4. items.a: 1. Scientific Reasons for Free vs Combined Existence: A. Elements Occurring in Combined State: • Causes: Elements that possess very low ionization energies (high electropositivity) or high electron affinities/electronegativity have incomplete valence shells and high chemical reactivity. They spontaneously lose, gain, or share electrons with surrounding oxygen, water, sulphur, or halogens to achieve stable noble gas octets and lower potential energy. • Examples: 1. Sodium (Na): Highly reactive alkali metal; exists as rock salt (NaCl), soda ash (Na2CO3), and Glauber's salt (Na2SO4·10H2O). 2. Calcium (Ca): Highly reactive alkaline earth metal; exists as limestone/marble (CaCO3) and gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O). B. Elements Occurring in Free (Native) State: • Causes: Elements that have completely filled valence electron shells (Noble gases) or very high ionization energies with low electropositivity and positive standard reduction potentials (Noble metals) do not readily react with oxygen, moisture, or environmental acids. They are thermodynamically stable in elemental form. • Examples: 1. Gold (Au): Noble precious metal that resists oxidation, corrosion, and acids, found as pure gold nuggets. 2. Helium / Argon (He, Ar): Noble gases with complete duplets/octets, existing as uncombined monoatomic atmospheric gases.

items.a: Three problem solving techniques: (1) Divide and conquer: break a big problem into smaller sub-problems; (2) Trial and error: try possible solutions until one works; (3) Algorithm / flowchart based step-by-step approach; (also working backwards, and using diagrams).

items.a: Q6 model: Step 1. Read N Step 2. Set F=1, K=1 Step 3. Repeat Steps 4 and 5 while K<=N Step 4. Set F=F*K Step 5. Set K=K+1 [End of while loop] Step 6. Write F Step 7. Exit (see Flowchart 12).

items.a: A flowchart is a diagram that shows the steps of an algorithm using symbols joined by arrows. Symbols: Terminal (oval) for start and end; Input/Output (parallelogram) for reading and displaying data; Process (rectangle) for calculations and assignment; Decision (diamond) for a yes/no or true/false test; Flow lines (arrows) for the direction; Connector (small circle) to join parts and an off-page connector.

items.q: Write an algorithm to calculate the factorial of a given number and draw flowchart for it.
items.q2: دیے گئے عدد کا فیکٹوریل معلوم کرنے کا الگورتھم لکھیں اور اس کا فلوچارٹ بنائیں۔
items.q3: د ورکړل شوي عدد د فکټوریل د محاسبې الګوریتم ولیکئ او فلوچارټ یې رسم کړئ.
items.a: Algorithm: 1. Start. 2. Read the number n. 3. Set fact = 1 and i = 1. 4. While i is not greater than n, set fact = fact x i and i = i + 1. 5. Display fact. 6. Stop. Flowchart: Start, input n, fact = 1, i = 1, decision (i <= n?): yes: fact = fact * i, i = i + 1, back to the decision; no: output fact, stop.

items.q: Write an algorithm and draw a flowchart to resolve quadratic equation.
items.q2: دو درجی مساوات حل کرنے کا الگورتھم لکھیں اور فلوچارٹ بنائیں۔
items.q3: د دوه درجه یي معادلې د حل الګوریتم ولیکئ او فلوچارټ یې رسم کړئ.
items.a: Algorithm: 1. Start. 2. Read a, b, c. 3. Calculate d = b x b - 4 x a x c. 4. If d < 0 display no real roots and go to step 7. 5. Calculate x1 = (-b + sqrt(d)) / (2a) and x2 = (-b - sqrt(d)) / (2a). 6. Display x1 and x2. 7. Stop. Flowchart: start, input a b c, process d, decision d < 0 (yes: message; no: compute x1 and x2 and output), stop.

items.q: Differentiate between compiler and interpreter.
items.q2: کمپائلر اور انٹرپریٹر میں فرق کریں۔
items.q3: د compiler او interpreter ترمنځ توپیر وکړئ.
items.a: A compiler translates the whole source program into machine code at once and then reports all errors; it runs fast afterwards (C, C++). An interpreter translates and executes the program one statement at a time and stops at the first error; it is slower in running (Python, BASIC).

items.q: Differentiate between program syntax and program semantic.

items.a: Syntax is the set of grammar rules for writing statements of a language (a missing semicolon is a syntax error); semantics is the meaning of the statements, i.e. what the statement does (a program with correct syntax but wrong logic has a semantic error).
items.h: Give short answers to the following questions.

items.q: Differentiate between Low level and high level languages.
items.q2: لو لیول اور ہائی لیول زبانوں میں فرق کریں۔
items.q3: د ټیټې او لوړې کچې ژبو ترمنځ توپیر وکړئ.
items.a: Low-level languages (machine and assembly) are close to the hardware, machine dependent, fast but difficult to write and learn. High-level languages (C, Python, Java) use English-like words, are machine independent, easy to learn and write, but must be translated into machine code.

items.a: OOP (Object-Oriented Programming) is a programming approach that organizes a program around objects, which combine data and the functions that work on it, using classes, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism (C++, Java).

items.a: High-level languages are easy to read and write (English-like), machine independent (portable), have fewer errors and are easy to debug, support structured programming and need a compiler or interpreter to translate them.

items.a: The source program is the program written by the programmer in a high-level language (a .c file); the object program is the machine-language form produced by the compiler (a .obj file) that is linked and run.

items.e: i: Syntax = rules for the structure of statements (like grammar); semantic = the meaning / steps a statement performs. ii: Low level languages are close to hardware (machine, assembly), hard for humans; high level languages are English-like, easy, machine independent and need a translator. iii: An IDE is software that brings editor, compiler, linker, debugger etc. into one environment to create, compile and run programs. iv: Object Oriented Programming builds programs from reusable objects (modules + data structures), e.g. C++, Java. v: Easy to learn, understand and write; easy to detect and remove errors; built-in library functions; machine independence. vi: A compiler translates the whole program at once into object code; an interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time. vii: A .h file of standard library function declarations, included with #include. viii: Source program

items.q: What is programming language? Explain different types of low level languages.
items.q2: پروگرامنگ زبان کیا ہے؟ لو لیول زبانوں کی مختلف اقسام کی وضاحت کریں۔

items.a: A programming language is a set of words and rules used to write instructions for a computer. Low-level languages: machine language is made of binary 0s and 1s directly executed by the CPU; assembly language uses short mnemonic codes (ADD, MOV) and needs an assembler to change it to machine code. They are fast and hardware dependent.

items.q: What are high level languages? Explain any five types of high level languages.
items.q2: ہائی لیول زبانیں کیا ہیں؟ ہائی لیول زبانوں کی کوئی سی پانچ اقسام کی وضاحت کریں۔

items.a: High-level languages are written in English-like words and are machine independent. Five types: C (a general purpose, structured language for system programs), C++ (object oriented), Java (portable, object oriented), Python (simple, popular for scripting and AI) and BASIC (easy for beginners); others are COBOL (business) and FORTRAN (science).

items.q3: header فایل څه دی؟
items.a: A header file has the declarations of library functions and macros (e.g. stdio.h for printf and scanf) and is added to the program with the #include directive before compiling.

items.q: What are reserved words?
items.q2: مخصوص الفاظ کیا ہیں؟
items.q3: ساتل شوې کلمې څه دي؟
items.a: Reserved words (keywords) are words with a fixed meaning in the language that cannot be used as names of variables, e.g. int, float, if, else, while, for, return.

items.q: What is the basic structure of C-program? Also explain different types of preprocessor directives.
items.q2: C پروگرام کا بنیادی ڈھانچہ کیا ہے؟ پری پروسیسر ڈائریکٹوز کی مختلف اقسام کی بھی وضاحت کریں۔
items.q3: د C پروګرام بنسټیز جوړښت څه دی؟ د preprocessor لارښوونو بېلابېل ډولونه هم تشریح کړئ.
items.a: A C program has: preprocessor directives (#include), the main function, braces, declarations of variables, and statements ending with semicolons, plus comments. Example: #include ; void main() { printf("Hello"); }. Preprocessor directives begin with # and are handled before compiling: #include adds a header file and #define defines a constant or macro; also #ifdef, #ifndef and #undef.

items.q: A quantity whose value may change during execution of the program is called a ______.
items.q2: وہ مقدار جس کی قدر پروگرام کے چلنے کے دوران بدل سکے ______ کہلاتی ہے۔ (الف) کانسٹنٹ (ب) متغیر (ج) نام (د) علامت
items.q3: هغه کمیت چې ارزښت یې د پروګرام د اجرا پر مهال بدلېدای شي ______ بلل کېږي. (الف) ثابت (ب) متغیر (ج) نوم (د) نښه
items.e: A variable is a quantity whose value may change while the program runs.

items.q: Write rules for variable names.
items.q2: متغیر ناموں کے قواعد لکھیں۔
items.q3: د متغیر نومونو قواعد ولیکئ.
items.a: Rules for variable names: begin with a letter or underscore, not a digit; use only letters, digits and underscore (no spaces or symbols); do not use a reserved word; C is case sensitive (Sum and sum differ); keep the name meaningful and not too long.
items.h: Give short answers to the following questions.

items.q: What are constants and variables? Differentiate them with examples.
items.q2: کانسٹنٹس اور متغیرات کیا ہیں؟ مثالوں سے ان میں فرق کریں۔
items.q3: ثابتونه او متغیرونه څه دي؟ په بېلګو یې توپیر وکړئ.
items.a: A constant is a fixed value that does not change during execution (5, 3.14, 'A', defined with const or #define). A variable is a named memory location whose value can change (int age = 15; age = 16;). A constant holds one value only, while a variable can be reassigned.

items.q: Explain different data types used in C-language with examples.
items.q2: C زبان میں استعمال ہونے والی مختلف ڈیٹا ٹائپس کی مثالوں سے وضاحت کریں۔
items.q3: په C ژبه کې کارېدونکي بېلابېل ډېټا ډولونه په بېلګو تشریح کړئ.
items.a: Data types in C: int (whole numbers, e.g. 25), float (real numbers with decimals, e.g. 3.14), double (larger precision decimals), char (a single character, e.g. 'A'), and void (no value). Examples: int age = 15; float price = 25.5; char grade = 'A';

items.q: What is type casting? Explain with examples.
items.q2: ٹائپ کاسٹنگ کیا ہے؟ مثالوں سے وضاحت کریں۔
items.q3: type casting څه دی؟ په بېلګو یې تشریح کړئ.
items.a: Type casting is converting a value from one data type to another. Implicit conversion is done by the compiler (int to float in mixed expressions); explicit casting is done by the programmer: float avg = (float) total / 3; or int x = (int) 7.9; which gives 7.

items.q: How variables are declared and initialized in C-language? Give examples.
items.q2: C زبان میں متغیرات کا اعلان اور ابتدائی قدر کیسے دی جاتی ہے؟ مثالیں دیں۔
items.q3: په C ژبه کې متغیرونه څنګه اعلان او پیلنی ارزښت ورکول کېږي؟ بېلګې ورکړئ.
items.a: A variable is declared by giving its data type and name: int a; float b; char c;. It is initialized by assigning a value, either at declaration (int a = 10;) or later (a = 10;); several variables can be declared together (int x, y, z;).

items.q3: په C ژبه کې هر بیان په ______ پای ته رسېږي. (الف) ټکی (ب) دوه ګونې quotes (ج) semicolon (د) کامه
items.e: Every C statement ends with a semicolon.

items.q: Why escape sequences are used? Give examples.
items.q2: ایسکیپ سیکوینسز کیوں استعمال ہوتے ہیں؟ مثالیں دیں۔
items.q3: escape sequences ولې کارېږي؟ بېلګې ورکړئ.
items.a: Escape sequences are special characters used inside strings to print things that cannot be typed directly: \n new line, \t tab, \b backspace, \\ backslash, \" double quote. Example: printf("Hello\nWorld"); prints on two lines.

items.q: What is the use of format specifiers? Give examples.
items.q2: فارمیٹ اسپیسیفائرز کا کیا استعمال ہے؟ مثالیں دیں۔
items.q3: د format specifiers کارونه څه ده؟ بېلګې ورکړئ.
items.a: A format specifier tells printf() and scanf() the type of data to print or read: %d for int, %f for float, %c for char, %s for string, %lf for double. Example: printf("%d", 25); prints 25 and printf("%f", 3.5); prints 3.500000.

items.q3: د *gets()* فنکشن موخه څه ده؟
items.a: The gets() function reads a whole line of text, including spaces, from the keyboard and stores it in a string (character array) until Enter is pressed. Example: char name[30]; gets(name);

items.q: Differentiate between *getch()* and *getche()* functions.

items.a: getch() reads one character from the keyboard without displaying it on the screen and without waiting for Enter; getche() also reads one character without Enter, but the character is displayed (echoed) on the screen.

items.q: What is output function? Describe in detail different types of output functions.
items.q2: آؤٹ پٹ فنکشن کیا ہے؟ آؤٹ پٹ فنکشنز کی مختلف اقسام تفصیل سے بیان کریں۔
items.q3: output فنکشن څه دی؟ د output فنکشنونو ډولونه په تفصیل بیان کړئ.
items.a: Output functions send data to the screen. printf() prints text and values with format specifiers, e.g. printf("Sum = %d", s); puts() prints a string followed by a new line; putchar() prints one character; putch() (conio.h) prints a character.

items.q: Discuss different format specifiers and escape sequences used in *printf()* function.
items.q2: *printf()* فنکشن میں استعمال ہونے والے مختلف فارمیٹ اسپیسیفائرز اور ایسکیپ سیکوینسز پر بحث کریں۔
items.q3: په *printf()* کې کارېدونکي format specifiers او escape sequences وڅېړئ.
items.a: Format specifiers in printf(): %d (int), %f (float), %c (char), %s (string), %lf (double), %u (unsigned). Escape sequences: \n (new line), \t (tab), \a (alert sound), \\ (backslash), \" (quote), \b (backspace). Example: printf("Name: %s\tAge: %d\n", name, age);

items.q: Explain different types of input functions with examples.
items.q2: ان پٹ فنکشنز کی مختلف اقسام کی مثالوں سے وضاحت کریں۔
items.q3: د input فنکشنونو ډولونه په بېلګو تشریح کړئ.
items.a: Input functions read data from the keyboard: scanf() reads formatted values, e.g. scanf("%d", &a); getchar() reads one character and waits for Enter; getch() and getche() read one character without Enter; gets() reads a whole line of text. Example: char c; c = getchar();

items.q: Write a program that reads three numbers and prints their sum, product and average.
items.q2: ایسا پروگرام لکھیں جو تین اعداد پڑھ کر ان کا مجموعہ، حاصلِ ضرب اور اوسط پرنٹ کرے۔
items.q3: پروګرام ولیکئ چې درې عددونه ولولي او مجموعه، حاصل ضرب او اوسط یې چاپ کړي.
items.a: #include ; void main() { int a, b, c, sum, product; float avg; printf("Enter three numbers: "); scanf("%d%d%d", &a, &b, &c); sum = a + b + c; product = a * b * c; avg = sum / 3.0; printf("Sum = %d Product = %d Average = %f", sum, product, avg); }

items.q: Differentiate between simple and compound assignment operators.
items.q2: سادہ اور کمپاؤنڈ اسائنمنٹ آپریٹرز میں فرق کریں۔
items.q3: د ساده او مرکب assignment operators توپیر وکړئ.
items.a: Simple assignment (=) stores a value in a variable (a = 5). Compound assignment operators combine an arithmetic operation with assignment (+=, -=, *=, /=, %=): a += 5 means a = a + 5.

items.q: What are operators? Explain different types of operators with examples.
items.q2: آپریٹرز کیا ہیں؟ مختلف اقسام کے آپریٹرز کی مثالوں سے وضاحت کریں۔
items.q3: operators څه دي؟ بېلابېل ډولونه یې په بېلګو تشریح کړئ.
items.a: Operators are symbols that perform operations on operands. Types: arithmetic (+ - * / %), relational (< > <= >= == !=), logical (&& and, double bar for or, ! not), assignment (= += -=), increment/decrement (++ --), and conditional (?:). Examples: a + b, a > b, (a > 5) && (b < 3), x += 2, i++.

items.q: Write a program in C to input three integers. Find out the largest among these integers using *if-else* structure and print it on the screen.

items.q3: په C کې د دریو integers د اخیستو پروګرام ولیکئ. د *if-else* په مرسته تر ټولو لوی ومومئ او چاپ یې کړئ.
items.a: #include ; void main() { int a, b, c; printf("Enter three integers: "); scanf("%d%d%d", &a, &b, &c); if (a >= b && a >= c) printf("%d is largest", a); else if (b >= c) printf("%d is largest", b); else printf("%d is largest", c); }

items.q: Write a program in C to input a single character and print a message "It is a vowel" or "It is a consonant". Use *if-else* structure.
items.q2: C میں ایک حرف ان پٹ کر کے "It is a vowel" یا "It is a consonant" پیغام پرنٹ کرنے کا پروگرام لکھیں۔ *if-else* استعمال کریں۔
items.q3: په C کې یو توری اخلئ او "It is a vowel" یا "It is a consonant" پیغام چاپ کړئ. *if-else* وکاروئ.
items.a: #include ; void main() { char ch; printf("Enter a character: "); scanf("%c", &ch); if (ch=='a' or ch=='e' or ch=='i' or ch=='o' or ch=='u' or the same five capitals) printf("It is a vowel"); else printf("It is a consonant"); } In C the word or is written as the logical OR operator (two vertical bars) between the comparisons; the capital letters are tested in the same way.

items.a: Loops repeat a block of statements. for loop: for(i = 1; i <= 5; i++) printf("%d ", i); (counted loop, initialization, condition and increment in one place). while loop: i = 1; while(i <= 5) { printf("%d ", i); i++; } (condition tested before each pass). do-while loop: i = 1; do { printf("%d ", i); i++; } while(i <= 5); (body runs at least once, condition tested after). All three print 1 2 3 4 5.

items.q: Differentiate between the *do-while* and *while* loops. Explain with program examples.

items.a: The while loop tests the condition first, so the body may never run; the do-while loop runs the body once before testing the condition at the end, so it executes at least once, and it ends with a semicolon. Example with i = 10: while(i < 5) prints nothing, but do { printf("%d", i); } while(i < 5); prints 10 once.

items.a: The three basic gates are AND, OR and NOT. AND: output 1 only when all inputs are 1 (A B: 00 gives 0, 01 gives 0, 10 gives 0, 11 gives 1). items.q: Convert the following Boolean expression to logic gate. f(A, B, C) = ABC+ ĀB̄ + C̄ + ĀB
items.q2: درج ذیل بولین اظہار کو لاجک گیٹ میں بدلیں۔ f(A, B, C) = ABC+ ĀB̄ + C̄ + ĀB
items.q3: لاندې بولین افاده منطقي دروازې ته واړوئ. f(A, B, C) = ABC+ ĀB̄ + C̄ + ĀB
items.a: f = ABC + A'B' + C' + A'B. Simplify: A'B' + A'B = A', so f = ABC + A' + C'. Since A' + ABC = A' + BC and C' + BC = C' + B, f = A' + B + C'. Gate diagram: NOT on A, NOT on C, and a three-input OR gate that takes A', B and C' (or the original expression with AND gates for ABC, A'B' and A'B joined to an OR gate with C').

items.q: What do you know about the Great bath of Mohenjodoro?

items.e: SpaceBook answer (pp. 71-72): about 12x7 m and 2.4 m deep with staircases at north and south; floor of fitted bricks with gypsum plaster and a bitumen layer for water-tightness; brick colonnades, doors, rooms and a well; probably used for social and religious bathing ceremonies.

items.e: SpaceBook answer (pp. 72-74): main stupa surrounded by 21 votive stupas; monastery with 28 student cells around a central pool, a second storey, Buddha statues, ventilators and lamp niches, kitchen and assembly hall; it served as a university.

items.q: Write a note on the importance of ancient historic places like Lahore Fort.
items.q2: لاہور کے قلعے جیسے قدیم تاریخی مقامات کی اہمیت پر نوٹ لکھیں۔
items.q3: د لاهور کلا په څېر د لرغونو تاریخي ځایونو د اهمیت په اړه یادښت ولیکئ.
items.a: They preserve history, art and identity.
items.e: SpaceBook answer (pp. 75-76): Lahore Fort records many eras — early references (11th century), damage by the Mongols and Timur, rebuilding in 1442, Mughal additions by Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb, Sikh pavilions and British changes; its gates, Diwan-i-Am, Moti Masjid, Naulakha and Sheesh Mahal show architecture and craft, attract visitors and teach history.

items.e: SpaceBook answer (pp. 76-77): built in seven years from about 1634-35 under Shah Jahan by Shaikh Ilm-ud-din Ansari (Wazir Khan) of Chiniot; inside the old city near Delhi Gate; includes a bazaar of 22 small shops.

items.q: What is the significance of Faisal Masjid?
items.q2: فیصل مسجد کی کیا اہمیت ہے؟
items.q3: د فیصل جومات اهمیت څه دی؟
items.a: National Mosque of Pakistan in Islamabad.
items.e: SpaceBook answer (pp. 77-78): designed by Vedat Dalokay (Aga Khan Award) like a Bedouin tent with four 260 ft minarets and no dome; funded by King Faisal, completed 1986; Sadequain's mosaics; holds 10,000 in the hall and about 300,000 in total — third largest capacity after Masjid al-Haram and Masjid an-Nabawi.

items.q: Write note on following! i. Minar-e-pakistan. ii. Illuminated manuscript. iii. Khat-e-Nastaleeq.
items.q2: درج ذیل پر نوٹ لکھیں: i۔ مینارِ پاکستان ii۔ منقش مخطوطہ iii۔ خطِ نستعلیق
items.q3: په لاندې یادښتونه ولیکئ: i. د پاکستان منار ii. ښکلې لاسي نسخه iii. نستعلیق خط
items.e: SpaceBook answer: (i) Minar-e-Pakistan — about 72 m tower in Iqbal Park, Lahore, where the Pakistan Resolution was passed on 23 March 1940; foundation 1960, completed 1968 for Rs 7.5 million; star-shaped base, 162-step stair, inscriptions of the Lahore Resolution. (ii) Illuminated manuscript — text decorated with ornamented initials, borders and miniatures; earliest AD 400-600; Muslim illuminators used floral designs and never figures in the Quran. (iii) Khat-e-Nastaleeq — Persian script style from 14th-15th century Iran, invented by Mir Ali Tabrizi, combining Naskh and Ta'liq; used for Urdu and Persian; Lahori style by Abdul Majeed Parveen Raqam.
